about: The speed timeline on the home page (`beta/landing.html`): five ways one game of Civilization VI gets played, and how many times faster each is than a person playing it by hand. `docs/SPEEDUP_TIMELINE.md` says how each stop is measured.

Operator 2026-11-22: "Above the 6 seconds video, lets have a timeline: right to left: 5 hrs for me to play a Civ 6 game, 10-15 minutes with CIVVIS computer control, how long with Firaxis Civ 6 Deity Sim? CIVVIS self-play should be down to 10s or so. Can scale across M5 Max cores to 1 game per second. which is on the left. We should track the multipliers for each one though and see how much we can push things. 1,000,000x speed imrpove would be a huge achievement over playing Civ 6 games. Provide a speedup number: Like 123,654x."

`stops` are listed slowest first as the operator listed them, and the first is the one the others are measured against. A stop's `readings` are its measurements, oldest first: `taken` the day, `seconds` the time one game takes, `from` how it was measured. The newest reading is the one shown; the older ones are the track of how far the stop has been pushed. A stop with `follows` keeps no readings: it is read from that ledger, one reading for every run that set a record.

`goals` are the multipliers the line is marked with, each under a `key` the pages name it by, and the line ends at the largest. The operator's on 2026-11-22 was a million ("1,000,000x speed imrpove would be a huge achievement"). A billion stood beside it from later that day ("Addd 1 billion x to the scaling scale as well") until 2026-11-24, when he took it off: "Change the timeline to just scale to 1,000,000x (drop the 1bX)." A stop's `goal_seconds` is its own target (the operator's "10s or so" for a self-play game and "1 game per second" across the cores).

`cloud` is what renting the rest of the way to a goal would cost (operator 2026-11-22: "we should also estimate the cloud cost in $ to fill i nthe remaining amount (note that this is a Fable 5.2 best estimate of the numbers)"). It is an estimate and not a measurement: nothing has been run in a cloud. Its entries are dated estimates, oldest first, the newest shown: who made it (`by`), the `machine` rented and its `cores`, the one-core stop whose game those cores play (`of`), the `single_thread` score of the machine's processor on the website of `data/performance/processors.json`, its list price for an hour (`dollars_an_hour`) and its spot price (`spot_dollars_an_hour`), and `from`, where each figure was read and what the estimate leaves out. A newer estimate is a new entry after the ones there. An entry whose `scaling` is `measured` does not take a rented machine's cores to play as fast as one core alone: it takes the share of that which our own every-core run reached, the only measurement of it there is. The entry of 2026-11-24 is the estimate worked out again when the operator asked for it: "reclauclate the cloud costs to make sure they are accurate."

`projected` are the stops past what was measured (operator 2026-11-22: "add to out speedup timeline: 10x theoretical scale up from local hardware ... hardware scaleup is to the left of m5 max. potential distributed RL fleet: up to 1000+x"). Nothing has run at one. Each names the measured stop it multiplies (`over`) and keeps dated `estimates`, oldest first, the newest shown: the day it was `taken`, the figure that stop's multiplier is multiplied by (`times`), `or_more` when the figure is open at its top (his "1000+"), and `from`, whose figure it is and what it stands for. A projected stop moves when the stop under it does, and it is never the page's number.

The CIVVIS Performance page (`beta/performance.html`) opens on the same readings as two tables with every calculation written out (operator 2026-11-22: "at the top of civvis performance we want to calculate a multiplier on the theoretical and experimetnal throughput of the simualtor. and the calculations. baeline is 5 hrs for manually played game. please add the deity computer control, deity self-play, civvis self-play."). Three keys are read by that page alone. A stop with `cores: 1` is the simulator on one core, so its speed can be multiplied across a machine's cores: that product is the theoretical throughput. A stop's `of` names the one-core stop whose game it plays on every core: its reading is the experimental throughput the theory is held against. `alone` on a one-core stop is a second list of readings, oldest first, of one game played with the machine to itself (`turns` played in `seconds`): the speed a core has when nothing else is running, which the busy host's readings are not.

Operator 2026-11-24, naming the stops: "on the speed timeline thing, we should have: human player 5 hrs, Firaxis Computer control: 10-15mins but we should benchmark this with our games, Firaxis self-play (test how long this take), CIVVIS self-play, "Parallel games, M5 Max, all 18 cores"." So the line's stops are those five. Firaxis computer control (`control`) is Civilization VI itself with CIVVIS at the controls of one seat, and Firaxis self-play (`firaxis_self_play`) is Civilization VI itself with Firaxis's own AI in every seat. A reading that is `worked` was worked out from other measurements and not timed itself, and the pages mark it so; a timed reading added after it takes its place. A stop with `line` false is kept off the home page's line and stays in the Performance page's tables: `deity_sim`, the simulator's game against rivals that play as Firaxis's AI does, which stood on the line as "Firaxis Civ 6 Deity sim" until the operator named the real game's self-play as the stop. `tournament` on a stop says the self-play tournament plays its game, so the Performance page's chart of that stop over time also draws the tournament's batches (`data/performance/self_play_times.json`). `benchmark` on a stop names a benchmark that keeps a record of its own, read when the site is published: `control` is the computer control games timed end to end by `beta/control_times.py` (operator 2026-11-24: "we should be benchmarking our civvis computer cnotrol games time end to end and that number show flow through to a performance chart"). Where the clone holds that record, its last seven days are the stop's newest reading and its days the stop's chart; the readings written here are what a clone without it shows.

A projected stop may stand on another projected stop listed before it (`over`): the M5 Max's theoretical most is ten times the irreducible game, which is ten times CIVVIS self-play, both the project owner's guesses of 2026-11-24. One that is `amortized` plays many games at once whatever it stands on.

A stop or a goal that is `amortized` plays many games at once, and its time is the time from one finished game to the next: the stopwatch's time over the games finished, which no single game takes (operator 2026-11-24: "starting left of CIVVIS self-play (but not including that), we should note that estimates are amortized games"). A projected stop is amortized when the stop it multiplies is. Every amortized entry has its games per second beside its time and leads with them (operator, the same day: "on the left side of the timeline, at more than 1 game / second, we should also provide the games per second as the standard measure and (time per game amoritized as the second measure)"; and later that day of the M5 Max's stop, which is under a game a second: "lest have m5 max blurb list amortiized games per second as the primary unit. as this is really amortiization at play"). A stop that is amortized has its goal worded in games a second too.

`line_to` is the multiplier the line runs out to, where that is past the largest goal (operator 2026-11-24: "maybe extend timeline out to 10,000,000x"). It is the line's end and no goal: nothing is aimed at it and nothing is costed to it. The million stands on the line at its own place, a tenfold short of the end, and the distributed fleet, which is past a million, stands on the line too, where it was an arrow off the end. Without `line_to`, or with one short of the largest goal, the line ends at the largest goal as it did.
Nothing derived is written here. `beta/speedup_timeline.py` works out every multiplier, text and place on the line when the site is published.

cloud.from: A best estimate by Claude Fable 5.2, the model that wrote this entry, asked for as one by the project owner. Not a quote, and nothing was run in a cloud. The machine is Amazon's c8a.48xlarge, its largest compute-optimized size on AMD's EPYC 9R45: 192 processors, each a whole core, and 384 GiB of memory. Its price was read on 2026-11-23 for US East (N. Virginia), Linux: $10.34592 an hour on demand, and $2.854 an hour on the spot market that day (other trackers showed $2.70 to $3.75). Its processor's score is PassMark's Single Thread Rating for the EPYC 9R45, read the same day from two samples with a high margin for error. One game on one of its cores is taken to be the one-core self-play reading, longer by the two processors' single thread scores, and every core is taken to play as fast as one, which the every-core run on the M5 Max came close to. The estimate leaves out storage, network traffic and the work of running such a fleet, counts whole machines, and assumes the price holds at any number of them, which no one has tested for the tens of thousands the larger goal needs.

A best estimate by Claude Fable 5.2, the model that wrote this entry, asked for as one by the project owner and worked out again on 2026-11-24 when he asked that the cost be checked. Not a quote, and nothing was run in a cloud. The machine is Amazon's c8a.48xlarge on AMD's EPYC 9R45: 192 processors, each a whole core, and 384 GiB of memory. Its price was read again on 2026-11-24 for US East (N. Virginia), Linux: $10.34592 an hour on demand, unchanged, and $2.876 an hour on the spot market that day ($2.854 the day before). Its processor's score is PassMark's Single Thread Rating for the EPYC 9R45, 3,812, read again the same day and still from two samples with a high margin for error. Two processors of the same generation with many samples bear it out when scaled to this one's 4.5 GHz: the EPYC 9575F (4,176 at 5.0 GHz, 40 samples) gives about 3,760 and the Ryzen 9 9950X (4,672 at 5.6 GHz, 683 samples) about 3,750. One game on one of its cores is the one-core self-play reading, longer by the two processors' single thread scores. What changed from the estimate before: a machine's cores are no longer taken to play as fast as one core does alone. The every-core run on the M5 Max is the only measurement of that there is, and it falls short of its cores times one core, so a rented machine is taken to reach the same share of its own. That may be hard on it: the M5 Max has cores of two speeds and had a held game and a browser beside the run, where a rented machine has cores of one kind and nothing else to do. The estimate leaves out storage, network traffic and the work of running a fleet, counts whole machines, and assumes the price holds for that many.

readings.from: The project owner's own figure for one game played by hand: five hours.

The middle game of the 238 complete Lv 8 (Deity) verification games played from 2026-11-16 to 2026-11-22 (results.jsonl on the ledger branch; a game recorded once, ending in a victory of ours or a rival's), each timed from the stamp in its tag to the stamp of its result. A tenth took under 10.1 minutes and a tenth over 16.3.

Benchmarked again with our own games on 2026-11-24: the middle game of the 324 complete Lv 8 (Deity) games of the seven days to that day (results.jsonl on the ledger branch at 4ffe6f9d; a game recorded once, ending in a victory of ours or a rival's), each timed from the stamp in its tag to the stamp of its result, so with Civilization VI launching, the game being set up and its ending. A tenth took under 9.8 minutes and a tenth over 16.1, and a game ended on turn 181 on average. Of the middle game of the forty newest, 48 s was setup, 239 s our own seat's turns, 409 s the turns of Firaxis's AI and 10 s the ending.

Worked out from our own games and not timed: no game has been played yet with Firaxis's AI in every seat on this setup. In the 40 newest complete Lv 8 (Deity) computer control games with a run folder (results 2026-11-23 17:22Z to 2026-11-24 14:48Z; six players, Continents, Online speed), the middle game's parts were 47.8 s of setup, 238.7 s of our own seat's turns, 409.4 s of Firaxis's AI playing its five seats with the city-states and barbarians, and 9.9 s of ending, 717.5 s in all over 180 turns. A game of that length with a sixth Firaxis seat in place of ours is the setup, the AI's turns and the ending: 467 s if the sixth seat cost nothing and 549 s if it cost a fifth more, and the slower is shown. Timing one needs the control harness to leave our seat to the game's own autoplay, which it cannot do yet.

Timed: one game of Civilization VI itself with Firaxis's own AI in every seat, played by the verification lane between two of its own games on 2026-11-24 (run firaxis-selfplay-20261124T174852Z, `tools/civ6_play.py --firaxis-self-play`). The lane's setup at Lv 8 (Deity): six players, Continents, a small map, Online speed, the control mod's time scale 3, our seat's view drawn. On its first turn the mod handed our seat to the game's autoplay manager and issued no order. Germany won a science victory on turn 171. The whole run took 331.9 s by the harness's run clock, the clock the computer control games are timed by: 48.0 s of setup, 275.2 s of play at 1.61 s a turn, and 8.7 s of ending. The machine's load was about 13 throughout, with the self-play tournament running beside it. It is one game, and a game's length moves with the turn it is won on.

Twelve games on one core, seeds 9101 to 9112, build a57ffc68: `gene_screen --jobs 1 --players 6 --width 74 --height 46 --city-states 9 --map continents --difficulty deity --rivals firaxis-faithful --handicap rivals --rival-chairs 5 --rival-rung -2 --rival-pace`. 349.7 s in all by the games' own `secs`, 19.6 s to 48.3 s a game, ending on turn 151 on average, every one by a science victory. Taken at nice 19 on a host at load 15 with a live Civilization VI game playing, so a quiet machine is faster.

Twelve games on one core, seeds 9101 to 9112, build d301d68d (main of 2026-11-24): `gene_screen --jobs 1 --players 6 --width 74 --height 46 --city-states 9 --map continents --difficulty deity --rivals firaxis-faithful --handicap rivals --rival-chairs 5 --rival-rung -2 --rival-pace`. 321.8 s in all by the games' own `secs`, 17.3 s to 49.8 s a game, ending on turn 154 on average. Every game was played to a victory and a Deity rival won each: eight by science, two by culture, two by religion. A turn took 174 ms, as much as a self-play turn the same day (178 ms): the game is shorter than a self-play game because it ends forty turns sooner, not because its turns are cheaper. Taken at nice 19 beside that day's self-play reading, on a host at load 12 with a live Civilization VI game and the tournament playing. The games' own `cpu_secs` come to 317.6 s, so the core was the game's for nearly all of the time.

alone.from: One standard self-play game with the machine to itself, build a57ffc68: 180 turns in 37 s, 4.9 turns a second. One seed, taken the day of the every-core record and written up with it (docs/GAMES_PER_MINUTE.md, "Eighteen games at once run slower than one alone").

readings.from: Twelve standard self-play games on one core, seeds 20261122000000 to 20261122000011, build a57ffc68: `gene_screen --jobs 1` with its defaults (six CIVVIS seats, nine city-states, 74x46 Continents, Online speed, 250 turns). 685.5 s in all by the games' own `secs`, 28.9 s to 102.8 s a game, ending on turn 192 on average. Taken at nice 19 on a host at load 15 with a live Civilization VI game playing, so a quiet machine is faster; a worker of the every-core benchmark, whose neighbours are all busy too, takes 59 s.

Twelve standard self-play games on one core, seeds 20261122000000 to 20261122000011, build d301d68d (main of 2026-11-24): `gene_screen --jobs 1` with its defaults (six CIVVIS seats, nine city-states, 74x46 Continents, Online speed, 250 turns). 414.0 s in all by the games' own `secs`, 18.0 s to 80.7 s a game with the middle game at 28.9 s, ending on turn 194 on average, 178 ms a turn. Taken at nice 19 beside that day's Deity sim reading, on a host at load 12 with a live Civilization VI game and the tournament playing. The games' own `cpu_secs` come to 408.3 s, so the core was the game's for nearly all of the time. The seeds are those of 2026-11-22 and the games are not: genes were added since, so a seed draws other genomes. With the shipped genome on every seat in place of a drawn one (`--deployment-genome`), the same seeds took 26.5 s a game right after, 17.8 s to 33.9 s, ending on turn 188 on average, 141 ms a turn.

estimates.from: The project owner's figure, 2026-11-24, and a guess by his own word: "somewhere to the left of CIVVIS self-play, through down Civ 6 Computationl Irreducability - ??? not sure where this is. Maybe just guess a 10x improvement?" One game on one core with nothing left in it that the game does not need, taken to be ten times as fast as CIVVIS self-play is today. A guess and not a run: nobody knows where it is. What a game takes now, in steps and instructions, is docs/PATH_STEPS.md.

The project owner's figure, 2026-11-24: "Maybe through down a "M5 Max, Theoretical Max Civ 6 Throughput" somewhere like 10x to the left of Civ 6 Computational Irr...". The most games one M5 Max could finish: the irreducible game on every core at once, taken to be ten times one such game on one core. A guess on a guess and not a run.

The project owner's figure, 2026-11-22: "10x theoretical scale up from local hardware". Ten times what the one M5 Max delivers with a game on every core, from larger hardware of our own. A calculation and not a run: no larger machine has played a game.

The project owner's figure, 2026-11-22: "potential distributed RL fleet: up to 1000+x". A thousand times the one M5 Max and more, from many machines playing self-play at once for reinforcement learning. A potential and not a run: no such fleet exists.
